turns.t: Come in, take a seat. The nurse has had a quick word and says you're here about your hair, but I'd rather hear it in your own words.
Yeah. It's thinning.
Thinning where, would you say? All over, or in one patch?
The top, mostly. The crown, where my parting is.
And how long have you noticed it for?
Six months. About that.
Was there something that made you spot it, or did it just creep up on you?
My wife pointed it out. Then I saw the photos from my sister's wedding and, well.
Right. Is it more that hairs are falling out, or that they're getting finer so you can see more scalp through them?
Both, a bit. It's coming out in handfuls when I wash it.
Handfuls in the shower. Is that every wash, or just now and then?
Every wash.

Okay. Think of your scalp like a lawn. Each hair grows for years, rests, drops out, and a new one starts from the same spot. Something can nudge a lot of them into the resting phase together, and then you lose a clump at once.
Right.
The other pattern is more like a lawn slowly going thin because every blade comes back a little finer each season. That one is down to the follicle itself.
Is that the one I've got?
I'd be guessing if I said, and I'd rather not guess at you. What I can tell you is that there are sensible things we can do whichever it turns out to be.
Okay.
Before anything else, a blood test makes sense. I'd like to check your iron stores and your thyroid, because both can quietly affect hair and both are easy to put right.
Fine. When would that be?
The nurse can take it on your way out today. It's about two minutes with a needle, no fasting needed.
Okay.
Meanwhile I'm going to start you on minoxidil foam. Carrying on with the lawn idea, it's a bit like fertiliser: it wakes the follicles up and lengthens their growing phase.
Do I put it on wet hair?
Dry scalp is best. Once a day, half a capful, rubbed in wherever it's thin, then wash your hands thoroughly.
Once a day. Right.
Be warned, it can make you shed a bit more for the first month or so. That's the old resting hairs making way, and it's a good sign rather than a bad one.
Hm. So worse first.
A little worse first, yes. Most people need around four months before they see any difference, so please don't judge it too early.
Four months.
Take a photo of your crown in the same light today, and then again every month. It's far more reliable than trusting your memory in the bathroom mirror.
I can do that.
And be kind to what you've got: no harsh brushing or tight hats. Ordinary shampoo is fine, you don't need anything fancy.
Not a problem.
Good. Did you want to ask me anything before you go?
Will the bloods take long to come back?
Usually a few days. The results will be on your record by then.
Right. Thanks, doctor.
You're welcome. Mind the step on your way out.
